sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Jagirdari Crisis**: The scarcity of 'Paibaqi' (land available for assignment) led to intense competition among the nobility, resulting in 'short-term' assignments and rack-renting of the peasantry.
• **Agrarian Distress**: Increased pressure on the peasantry to maximize revenue led to widespread peasant uprisings (Jats, Satnamis, Sikhs) and abandonment of cultivation.
• **Commercial Decentralization**: As the central authority weakened, trade routes became less secure, leading to the rise of 'local protectionism' and the emergence of powerful regional banking houses (e.g., Jagat Seths).
• **Key Metric**: The 'Revenue-to-Expenditure' gap widened, forcing the state to rely on 'Ijaradari' (revenue farming), which replaced the traditional administrative collection.

sections.title: Comprehensive Classification & Comparative Matrix
rows: Shift from Zabt to Ijaradari (Revenue Farming); focus on cash crops.
Fiscal desperation of the state and nobility.
Mains: Impact on peasant mobility and rural stratification.
Rise of regional trade hubs (Murshidabad, Hyderabad, Awadh).
Shift of political power from Delhi to provincial capitals.
Prelims: Role of European Trading Companies in filling the vacuum.

items.definition: The system of revenue farming where the right to collect revenue was auctioned to the highest bidder, leading to the exploitation of the peasantry.
Land kept in reserve by the state for assignment as Jagirs; its depletion was a primary indicator of the Jagirdari crisis.

items.title: Major Applications / Initiatives
items.content:
• **Regional Autonomy**: Successor states (Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad) maintained economic stability by localizing revenue collection.
• **Banking Networks**: The rise of indigenous bankers (Sahukars) who financed both the state and the European companies.

items.title: Challenges & Way Forward
items.content:
• **Key Challenges**: Breakdown of the 'All-India' market, increased cost of protection for trade, and political instability.
• **Solutions**: Regional states adopted more pragmatic revenue policies to ensure long-term agricultural productivity.

items.title: Mnemonic for Retention
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym**: 'J-I-P' (Jagirdari Crisis -> Ijaradari -> Peasant Distress).
• **Decoded Meaning**: The sequence of economic decay: Jagirdari crisis caused the state to adopt Ijaradari, which ultimately caused Peasant distress.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: Do not assume the 18th century was a period of 'total economic collapse'. While the central Mughal economy declined, regional economies (like Bengal) were often prosperous.
Mains Value Addition: Use the term 'Economic Decentralization' rather than 'Economic Collapse' to show a nuanced understanding of the 18th-century transition.

keyTakeaways: The 18th century was a period of transition, not just decline.
Ijaradari was the institutional response to the fiscal crisis of the Mughal state.
Regional successor states became the new centers of economic gravity.
